source.title: Averaging Weights Leads to Wider Optima and Better Generalization
source.authors: Pavel Izmailov; Dmitrii Podoprikhin; T. Garipov; D. Vetrov; A. Wilson

record.file_problem: none; full paper text supplied, though some figures are described only through captions and plotted curves.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own weight perturbation and train/test surface comparisons, arguing that wider solutions can improve generalization but that the relationship is conditional and asymmetric; it also finds conventional SGD optima can have steep directions.
record.gate_note: The study tests the gap between training and test performance through SWA-versus-SGD comparisons and learning-rate settings. Table 1–2 accuracy results also test generalization, but do not report paired training error and are not extracted as gap rows. FGE comparisons and cited prior results are not rows. Figure 6 and Figure 7 curves are described, but precise values are not recoverable from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study measures SWA performance and unscaled weight-space geometry. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap ranking, and its experiments do not test any other listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: averaging SGD weights collected with cyclical or constant learning rates finds more central, flatter solutions and improves test performance across the tested architectures, sometimes with slightly worse training loss. The authors use optima to mean procedure-converged solutions rather than distinct local minima.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies stochastic weight averaging and its geometry, not the original claim's random-label memorization setup or the V7 magnitude-aware sharpness measurement. It compares SWA against conventional SGD across image-classification models and learning-rate schedules.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning-rate schedule and training epoch affect SWA convergence and reported test error; the paper reports that more aggressive constant learning rates generally converge faster and intermediate rates usually give the best results.

fits_no_version.finding: SWA solutions tolerate larger unscaled random perturbations than SGD solutions; connecting-line comparisons show shifted training-loss and test-error surfaces and steep ascent near SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight averaging can find flatter regions within the same basin with improved test performance.

fits_no_version.finding: SWA convergence and test performance depend on learning-rate schedule and training duration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning-rate choices affect the performance of stochastic weight averaging.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-100, constant-learning-rate Wide ResNet training yields 81.7% SWA accuracy while individual averaged trajectory models remain near 65%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Averaging weights can substantially outperform individual constant-learning-rate trajectory models.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence
record.problems: Geometry results are largely qualitative plots, with no exact curve values for the perturbation comparisons. Figure 4 uses 10 random directions, and the authors note the loss and test-error surfaces are shifted; the reported width evidence is not the magnitude-aware sharpness measure in V7. The reported accuracy averages in Table 1 use three runs, while ImageNet reports mean and standard deviation over three runs.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 2 report SWA, SGD and FGE test accuracies for many architecture-budget combinations, but these are not paired training-versus-test error measurements and do not map to any of the listed versions. Figure 2 and Figure 3 provide trajectory/test-error and train-loss visualizations but no separable numerical outcomes for each point or schedule. FGE values are cited from prior work.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Width scaling beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations; large-batch SWA is proposed as future work.
Dropout ablations, training-set-size dependence, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test error gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's designation of V7 as tested conflicts with its own correctly unlinked rows. General flatness evidence does not test the specifically magnitude-aware claim. Tables 1–2 are declared in rows_left_out and require no missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width scaling beyond interpolation in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout's effect on test error and its interaction with training set size or augmentation.
The magnitude-aware perturbation measure and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures; no tested comparison here uses that version's stated measure.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: Preactivation ResNet-164
rows.operation_detail: Compared test error and L2-regularized cross-entropy train loss along random unit-sphere weight perturbation rays from SWA and conventional SGD solutions.

conditions.value: 10 random directions from a uniform distribution on the unit sphere

rows.measure: Test error and L2-regularized cross-entropy train loss as perturbation distance increases
rows.baseline: Conventional SGD solution; exact value not stated for the curves
rows.value: SWA curves are considerably wider; for any shown random direction from SGD, test error increases
rows.note: The paper describes qualitative width differences but this random-direction perturbation result does not establish the V7 magnitude-aware sharpness measure or its ranking of generalization gaps.
rows.check: Random unit-sphere perturbations are not scaled to weight magnitudes; the curves measure regularized training loss and test error rather than V7's perturbation tolerance and generalization gap.

rows.subject: Preactivation ResNet-164
rows.operation_detail: Compared train loss and test error along the line segment connecting SWA and SGD weights.

conditions.value: line segment connecting SWA and SGD solutions

rows.measure: L2-regularized cross-entropy train loss and test error along the connecting line
rows.baseline: SGD endpoint; exact curve value not stated
rows.value: SWA endpoint has considerably lower test error; train-loss and test-error curves are shifted; SGD lies near the boundary of a wide flat region of train loss and loss is steep near SGD
rows.note: The paper states that SGD train loss is slightly lower than SWA and test error is lower by 1.5% at the converged value, but does not give the curve's absolute values. The result discusses generalization geometry, not V7's magnitude-aware measure.
rows.check: Connecting-line geometry does not measure V7. Remove the note's attribution of a 1.5-percentage-point benefit to this comparison: that number appears in the Figure 4 discussion, where the text says SGD has lower test error, contradicting the surrounding account that SWA has lower test error. The exact difference is therefore ambiguous.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Compared train loss and test error along the line segment connecting SWA and SGD weights.

conditions.value: line segment connecting SWA and SGD solutions

rows.measure: L2-regularized cross-entropy train loss and test error along the connecting line
rows.baseline: SGD endpoint; exact curve value not stated
rows.value: Figure shows a shifted train-loss and test-error surface and the paper's text says the plotted networks exhibit the same-basin, flatter-SWA pattern
rows.note: The text's qualitative account is stated for Figure 5; separate numerical values for VGG-16 are not given.
rows.check: The qualitative connecting-line comparison is accurately described but does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or rank generalization gaps.

rows.subject: Preactivation ResNet-164
rows.operation_detail: Compared SWA and conventional SGD test error under different constant and cyclical learning-rate schedules, starting from the same 125-epoch SGD initialization.

conditions.value: model trained for 125 epochs using conventional SGD

rows.baseline: Fully trained conventional SGD for 150 epochs
rows.value: Figure 6 reports curves only; text says more aggressive constant learning rate generally leads to faster SWA convergence, and an intermediate learning rate usually gave the best results
rows.note: The learning-rate curves show schedule dependence, but exact plotted test-error values are not stated.
rows.check: Change partial to cannot_determine: learning-rate dependence of SWA accuracy does not establish a partial effect for any listed version. This is a comparison of the study's own method across schedules.

rows.subject: Wide ResNet-28-10
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed learning rate 0.05 and averaged weights from the end of each epoch from epoch 140 through epoch 300.
rows.measure: Test accuracy of SWA model and individual models on the averaged trajectory
rows.baseline: Individual models along the trajectory have accuracy approximately 65%
rows.value: Final SWA model test accuracy was 81.7; individual models' accuracy stayed at approximately 65%
rows.note: This reports a generalization outcome under constant-learning-rate SWA, but does not measure the V7 magnitude-aware property or its relationship to the train-test gap.
rows.check: The reported 81.7% versus approximately 65% accuracy comparison concerns SWA versus its individual trajectory models and bears on no listed version.

rows.subject: Preactivation ResNet-164
rows.operation_detail: Trained with fixed learning rate 0.1 and averaged weights beginning at epoch 200.
rows.baseline: Conventional SGD with decaying learning rate; exact value not stated
rows.value: Figure 9 reports curves only; exact errors not stated
rows.note: The figure caption describes constant-learning-rate SWA and SGD curves; there is no corresponding numeric test-error value in the text.
rows.check: This is a performance comparison of the study's own method; neither the measure nor the experimental manipulation tests a listed version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
